Grading note for sub-item 1b (HashMap is mutable):

Award the point whenever the answer conveys that a HashMap can be modified, by whatever wording it uses. The literal term "mutable" is not required: any stated property of HashMap that amounts to modifiability counts, such as noting that it supports `put`, `remove`, or `clear`, that entries can be added after construction, or that its contents can be changed/updated. Treat such functional descriptions as fully equivalent to the word "mutable" and do not deduct merely because the formal term is absent.

Deduct 1 point only if the answer states no such property at all — i.e., it never indicates, in any form, that a HashMap can be modified or that its contents can be added to, removed from, or otherwise changed.

Award no_deduct only if the answer contains an explicit statement of cardinality — that the singleton map contains/returns exactly one key-value pair, holds only a single mapping, has one entry, or that its size is always 1. The statement does not have to be a separate sentence or a separate point from the immutability discussion: a combined phrase such as "Collections.singletonMap returns an immutable map with one entry" satisfies this item even though the same clause is also credited for 1a. Nor does the cardinality have to be grammatically predicated of singletonMap itself; the fact may be carried indirectly, e.g. by describing the HashMap wrapper as "a new, mutable HashMap instance initialized with the single entry from the singleton map" or "creates a mutable HashMap by copying the single entry." No comparison to HashMap is required — the answer need not say that a HashMap can hold arbitrarily many entries; stating the single-mapping fact about singletonMap alone is enough.

In particular, merely using the name "singletonMap," showing or quoting a `Collections.singletonMap(k, v)` call, or saying only that "you cannot add more entries to it" does not convey the cardinality and is deducted.

**Sub-item 2c — "discusses usages of the map argument within messageParams, noting that these are read-only."**

Award the point whenever the answer clearly establishes that the map argument is only read and never mutated inside `messageParams`. The read-only determination itself is what counts as "discussing the usages" — the answer does not have to enumerate the individual call sites, operations, or lines where the map is touched. A bare but unambiguous conclusion such as "the map is only read; nothing in `messageParams` modifies it" is sufficient. The same holds when the read-only nature is clearly implied by the answer's reasoning about how the map is used rather than asserted as a standalone sentence — e.g., "passing `Collections.singletonMap` here is safe because nothing in `messageParams` ever calls `put` or `remove` on it," or "no `UnsupportedOperationException` will be thrown since the map is only queried." An incorrect determination fails the requirement to note that the usages are read-only, so this deduction applies independently of, and in addition to, any deduction taken under the separate "incorrectly states that the usages modify it" sub-item.
2d:
**Sub-item 2d (penalty item, −2):** Apply this deduction only when the answer makes an explicit, unhedged, committed assertion that code inside `messageParams` itself writes to / mutates the very map object that was passed in as the argument — e.g. "messageParams calls `put`/`remove`/`clear` on the map", "the method modifies the passed map", "the usages inside messageParams add entries to the map you supply." All three conditions must hold together: the claim must be about the direct map argument as used inside `messageParams` (not some other map object), it must explicitly assert that a mutation actually occurs there (not merely imply one), and it must be stated without hedging.

Do **not** deduct in any of the following cases. (a) Scope: the answer says `messageParams` copies the entries into a new map that is then modified, that the map is stored and mutated later by other code, or that some method called downstream mutates its own map — these are not claims about the usages inside `messageParams`. (b) Implication without assertion: the answer only says things like "messageParams requires a mutable map", "an immutable map won't work here", or "a write to the map would throw `UnsupportedOperationException`", without asserting that such a write actually occurs in `messageParams`. (c) Hedging: the claim is qualified with "may", "might", "it is possible that", "one of these could be", or mutation is listed as one hypothesis among several without being endorsed.

In short: deduct 2 points only for a flat, unqualified statement that the code within `messageParams` mutates the passed-in map object itself; in every other case, no deduction under this item.
